title: The Fresnel lens
hook: Lighthouses shone farther once someone cut their big lens into thin rings.
peek: A lens powerful enough for a lighthouse would be huge, heavy and thick. In the 1820s Augustin Fresnel kept only the curved surface that bends the light and arranged it as rings, and his lenses still turn in lighthouses today.
lede: A lens bends light only at its surfaces, so most of the glass inside a thick lens is dead weight. The French engineer Augustin Fresnel saw that a big lens could be cut into a set of thin concentric rings, each shaped like a slice of the original curve. The result was flatter, lighter and much brighter than the mirrors lighthouses had used.

bullets.text: Fresnel's first lighthouse lens was installed in 1823 at Cordouan, at the mouth of the Gironde in France. The new light was far brighter than the old mirrors, and over the following decades lighthouse services in other countries switched to his lenses.

For the light that escaped above and below the central rings, Fresnel added prism rings that bounced it back into the beam. A first-order lens gathers nearly all of a lamp's light into one strong horizontal beam.

Fresnel was not the first to think of it. In the 1700s the naturalist Buffon proposed carving a lens in steps, but making one from a single piece of glass was impractical. Fresnel built his from separate rings.

Fresnel lenses came in orders by size. The largest, first order, stood taller than a person and was used on major coasts, while small sixth-order lenses marked harbours. The same ring idea now appears in car headlights and overhead projectors.
